questions.q: Per this lesson, what is the real test of a CSDM implementation at enterprise scale?
options: Whether the original implementation team modeled it correctly on day one
Whether it stays correctly modeled as dozens of teams who weren't part of the original design keep touching it over years
Whether it was documented in a single slide deck at rollout
Whether the Business Service layer was configured before the Technical Service layer
questions.explain: Getting the model right once is achievable; the real challenge is whether it stays consistent as many teams independently maintain it for years afterward.

questions.q: What does this lesson say happens to CMDB data quality without deliberate, ongoing governance?
options: It stays stable indefinitely on its own, with no active effort required
It only degrades if Discovery is disabled
It improves automatically as more teams use the CMDB
It erodes gradually and predictably — through inconsistent classification, stale relationships, duplicate CIs, and silent scope creep
questions.explain: Data quality erodes unless something actively pushes back — the lesson names several concrete, cumulative failure modes.

questions.q: Why does a decommissioned server's relationship to a Business Service often stay in the CMDB after the server is gone?
options: Because Business Services cannot have Technical Service relationships
Because stale relationships automatically self-correct within 90 days
Because ServiceNow does not allow relationships to be removed
Because removing the relationship wasn't anyone's explicitly assigned job
questions.explain: This is a named example of drift: a stale relationship persists because no one owned the responsibility of cleaning it up.

questions.q: What does this lesson say an architect's CSDM responsibility actually shifts to at enterprise scale?
options: Disabling CI creation for every team except the original implementation team
Designing the ongoing governance process — stewardship, change discipline, recurring audits, and a feedback loop into the model
Replacing CSDM with a simpler, ungoverned data model
Personally re-classifying every CI across every team
questions.explain: The architect's job shifts from designing the model once to designing the process that keeps dozens of teams consistent with it over years.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a team's workaround or shortcut deserves a feedback loop back into the model, rather than just being blocked?
options: Because governance should never involve reviewing team behavior
Because the CSDM model can never be changed once implemented
Because workarounds should always be adopted platform-wide without review
Because a team's shortcut can signal a real gap in the model that deserves a deliberate, centralized fix rather than being quietly copied uncorrected
questions.explain: Governance isn't pure enforcement — a recurring workaround can be a legitimate signal that the model itself needs a deliberate update.
